E1: (1) A ProximityPrompt only shows when it has a world position. That means its parent must be a BasePart, an Attachment, or a Model with a PrimaryPart. Here the parent is a Folder inside a Model that has no PrimaryPart, so the prompt has no position and never shows. Fix: move the prompt under a part of the machine (or an Attachment in that part), or set VendingMachine.PrimaryPart and parent the prompt to the model. (2) RequiresLineOfSight defaults to true. The engine casts a ray from the camera to the prompt's parent, and the glass case blocks that ray, so the prompt is hidden. Fix: set RequiresLineOfSight = false, or put the prompt on an Attachment or part outside the glass. You could also set the glass's CanQuery = false so the line-of-sight check ignores it, but that hides the glass from all raycasts.
E2: AlwaysOnTop = false: the tag is then depth-tested and hidden behind walls. True draws it over all 3D geometry. MaxDistance = 100: the tag is not rendered beyond 100 studs from the camera (0 means unlimited). Size: use scale instead of offset, for example UDim2.fromScale(4, 1). On a BillboardGui, scale is measured in studs, so the tag acts like a real object and gets smaller with distance. Offset is fixed screen pixels, which is why the tags stay the same size. Optional: use StudsOffset or ExtentsOffsetWorldSpace to lift the tag above the head. With a scale size, set TextScaled on the labels so the text resizes with the tag. Leave LightInfluence at 0 if the tags should not darken in shadow.
E3:
When CharacterAutoLoads is false, Roblox no longer spawns characters at all: not on join and not after death. RespawnTime is only used by the automatic respawn, so it has no effect now. The server has to spawn characters itself:
```lua
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
Players.CharacterAutoLoads = false
Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(function(p)
  p.CharacterAdded:Connect(function(char)
    char:WaitForChild("Humanoid").Died:Connect(function()
      task.wait(3)
      if p.Parent then p:LoadCharacter() end -- or LoadCharacterAsync if available
    end)
  end)
  p:LoadCharacter()
end)
```
In a round-based game, call LoadCharacter when the round logic wants the player spawned instead of straight away. Also loop over players already in the server, in case some joined before the script connected.
E4: CanQuery = false removes a part from all spatial queries: Raycast, Blockcast, Shapecast and the GetPartsIn* overlap queries. The ray cannot hit the glass whatever the filter says. CanQuery can only be turned off when CanCollide is also false, which is exactly this setup. Fix: set CanQuery = true on the glass and keep CanCollide = false so players still walk through. The laser then hits it (RaycastParams.RespectCanCollide defaults to false, so non-collidable parts are still hit). If other queries must ignore the glass, filter it out per query with RaycastParams/OverlapParams (an exclude list or a CollisionGroup) instead of turning off CanQuery.
E5: Error 1: Clone() returns nil when Archivable = false, so g is nil and g:PivotTo fails. Fix: set Archivable = true on the template and its descendants (non-archivable descendants are silently left out of the clone), or set it to true just before cloning. Error 2: Destroy() sets Parent to nil and permanently locks the Parent property, disconnects the instance's connections and destroys its descendants. A destroyed instance cannot be reused. Correct pattern: keep one archivable template that never goes into the world (ServerStorage is best for server-only spawning). Clone it for every spawn, set the clone's pivot, parent the clone last, and Destroy the clone when the goblin dies. If you need pooling, park pooled clones (Parent = nil or a storage folder) instead of destroying them. Never destroy the template.

E8:
```lua
local function swing(attackerChar)
  local hrp = attackerChar:FindFirstChild("HumanoidRootPart")
  if not hrp then return end
  local params = OverlapParams.new()
  params.FilterType = Enum.RaycastFilterType.Exclude
  params.FilterDescendantsInstances = {attackerChar}
  local cf = hrp.CFrame * CFrame.new(0, 0, -3)
  local parts = workspace:GetPartBoundsInBox(cf, Vector3.new(6, 5, 6), params)
  local hit = {}
  for _, part in parts do
    local model = part:FindFirstAncestorOfClass("Model")
    local hum = model and model:FindFirstChildOfClass("Humanoid")
    if hum and not hit[hum] and hum.Health > 0 then
      hit[hum] = true
      hum:TakeDamage(20)
    end
  end
end
```
The hit table makes sure each humanoid takes damage at most once per swing. Caveat: GetPartBoundsInBox tests each part's axis-aligned bounding box, not its real shape. Rotated or thin parts can register as hits slightly outside the box. If you need exact geometry, use GetPartsInPart with a box part, which is slower. The query is also one snapshot on the server, so with latency the result can differ a little from what the client saw.

```lua
local template = game.ServerStorage.Tree
local function placeTree(hitPos: Vector3)
  local tree = template:Clone()
  tree:ScaleTo(tree:GetScale() * 1.5)
  local _, size = tree:GetBoundingBox()
  local pivotOffset = tree:GetPivot().Position.Y - (tree:GetBoundingBox().Position.Y - size.Y/2)
  local rot = CFrame.Angles(0, math.rad(math.random(0, 359)), 0)
  tree:PivotTo(CFrame.new(hitPos + Vector3.new(0, pivotOffset, 0)) * rot)
  tree.Parent = workspace
end
```
ScaleTo scales parts, joints, attachments, meshes, particles and so on as one unit. PivotTo works without a PrimaryPart, using the model's WorldPivot. The offset puts the base of the bounding box on the hit point. Older approaches to avoid: SetPrimaryPartCFrame/GetPrimaryPartCFrame are deprecated, need a PrimaryPart and drift with floating-point error. Model:MoveTo avoids collisions and can push the tree up onto other geometry. Resizing each part's Size and Position by hand breaks welds, attachments, mesh scale and offsets. Old ResizeIncrement and manual-weld tricks are unnecessary now.
E11: Use MemoryStoreService for both. 1v1 queue: a MemoryStoreQueue (AddAsync / ReadAsync with an invisibility timeout / RemoveAsync to acknowledge) or a MemoryStoreSortedMap keyed by join time or skill. One server pops two entries, calls TeleportService:ReserveServer and tells the players' servers through MessagingService (or a shared map entry) so they TeleportAsync to the reserved server. Hourly top 100: a MemoryStoreSortedMap per hour (for example 'scores_<hourIndex>') with an expiration of about 1-2 h. Write with UpdateAsync keeping the max score, read with GetRangeAsync(Descending, 100). If the board must persist, use OrderedDataStore instead (slower, tighter limits). Limits that shape the design: a memory quota of about 64 KB + 1 KB per user across the experience; request units of about 1000 + 100 x CCU per minute experience-wide, plus per-partition throughput limits; item size up to about 32 KB; key length 128 chars; maximum expiration 45 days; GetRangeAsync returns at most 200 items per call; queue invisibility timeouts. Keep entries small, use expirations, shard hot keys, and retry with backoff. MessagingService has its own limits (1 KB messages, publish and subscribe rate caps).
E12: Per-server budgets per minute (classic standard DataStore): GetAsync 60 + 10 x players; Set/Increment/Update 60 + 10 x players; GetSorted (ordered) 5 + 2 x players; Remove 60 + 10 x players. For 40 players that is 460 per minute. UpdateAsync uses both a Get and a Set request. Your load is about 40 updates per minute from autosave plus saves on leave, which fits comfortably, but check DataStoreService:GetRequestBudgetForRequestType before saving and queue when the budget is low. On shutdown, BindToClose gets about 30 s to save everyone. Per-key limits: writes to the same key need about 6 s between them (faster writes are queued or throttled, so do not save on leave in the same second as an autosave); value size up to 4 MB serialized (JSON); key names and DataStore names up to 50 characters; metadata limits; per-key throughput of about 25 MB/min read and 4 MB/min write. Use session locking (for example a lock field inside UpdateAsync) so that two servers do not overwrite each other when a player hops servers. Use pcall with exponential backoff. Note: in 2026 Roblox moved toward experience-level throughput and storage quotas, so check the current docs.
E13: On the server, call TextService:FilterStringAsync(name, ownerUserId, Enum.TextFilterContext.PublicChat) inside a pcall. Because everyone sees the name, use TextFilterResult:GetNonChatStringForBroadcastAsync(). That gives the strictest result and is the right one for non-chat text shown to all users. Show only the filtered string (for example in the BillboardGui). If filtering fails or errors, show nothing or a placeholder such as a default name, never the raw text. Never filter on the client or trust a client-filtered string. Persistence: save the raw name to the DataStore, and filter it again every time it is loaded and shown, because filter rules and the viewer's context change. Never show stored text without filtering it again. Also enforce a length limit, rate-limit rename requests, and strip control characters on the server.
E14: External side: your bot calls the Open Cloud MessagingService API with POST https://apis.roblox.com/messaging-service/v1/universes/{universeId}/topics/{topic}, header x-api-key: <key>, Content-Type: application/json, and body {"message": "<text or JSON string>"} (up to 1 KB). Credentials: create an API key on the Creator Dashboard (Open Cloud) with the Messaging Service API 'publish' permission, scoped to that experience. Restrict it with an IP allowlist and an expiration, and keep it in the bot's secrets, never in game code. In-game side: every server script calls MessagingService:SubscribeAsync(topic, function(msg) ... end) at startup (inside a pcall). It reads msg.Data, validates or sanitises it, then FireAllClients through a RemoteEvent (or uses TextChatService system messages) to show the banner. Delivery is best effort, near real time (within seconds), with no guarantee and no history, so a server that starts later misses it. If late joiners must also see it, also store the announcement in a DataStore or MemoryStore through Open Cloud. Mind the subscription and publish rate limits.
E15: Building: set the model's ModelStreamingMode = Atomic. The model and all its descendants then stream in together once any part is needed, so the LocalScript never sees half of it (wait for it with WaitForChild on the model). Otherwise the client receives parts piecemeal, and with plain WaitForChild on every part a script can hang. Player:RequestStreamAroundAsync(position) (server, or client for its own player) can pre-load an area. Scoreboard: set ModelStreamingMode = Persistent. It is sent to every client at join and never streamed out, so UI code can always rely on it. PersistentPerPlayer plus Model:AddPersistentPlayer(player) does the same for chosen players only. Workspace settings that matter: StreamingMinRadius and StreamingTargetRadius, StreamOutBehavior (LowMemory or Opportunistic) and StreamingIntegrityMode (PauseOutsideLoadedArea). Trade-offs: Atomic sends a large model in one burst and keeps all of it while it is streamed in. Persistent models always use client memory and bandwidth and slow down join, and the client still has to wait for them at first (wait on the model; it may not be there the instant a script runs). Overusing either one defeats the purpose of streaming. Still write code that checks for nil.
E16: Aim direction: yes, switch it to UnreliableRemoteEvent. It is high-frequency, only the latest value matters, and a dropped or out-of-order packet is harmless because the next update replaces it. Hit reports: no, keep a reliable RemoteEvent. Hits are discrete, important events that must arrive exactly once, and they must still be validated on the server (rate, distance, line of sight, ammo, fire timing). Limits of UnreliableRemoteEvent: delivery and order are not guaranteed. Each payload is limited to roughly 900-1000 bytes; larger payloads are dropped rather than split, so send compact data (for example a Vector3 or a buffer, not tables of strings). There are no return values (it is fire-only, like RemoteEvent). Remotes are also throttled overall, so 30 Hz per player is fine, but rate-limit and sanity-check the values on the server, and consider sending only when the aim changes meaningfully.
E17:
```lua
-- 2 + 4*3 = 14 bytes
local function pack(id: number, pos: Vector3): buffer
  local b = buffer.create(14)
  buffer.writeu16(b, 0, id)
  buffer.writef32(b, 2, pos.X)
  buffer.writef32(b, 6, pos.Y)
  buffer.writef32(b, 10, pos.Z)
  return b
end
local function unpack(b: buffer): (number, Vector3)
  return buffer.readu16(b, 0), Vector3.new(buffer.readf32(b, 2), buffer.readf32(b, 6), buffer.readf32(b, 10))
end
-- server: remote:FireAllClients(pack(id, part.Position))
-- client: remote.OnClientEvent:Connect(function(b) local id, pos = unpack(b) end)
```
Rules relied on: a buffer has a fixed size set at creation and cannot grow. Offsets are zero-based byte offsets. Reads and writes outside the buffer throw. Values are little-endian. writeu16 truncates the number to 16 bits (0-65535). f32 loses precision compared with Luau's f64 numbers. Buffers are mutable and passed by reference inside one VM, but copied when sent over a remote. Buffers replicate efficiently as raw bytes.
E18: Every unanchored assembly is simulated by one machine, its network owner. By default the server automatically gives ownership to the nearest player, or keeps it. When the driver sits in a VehicleSeat, the engine normally gives that player ownership, but the auto-assignment can hand it back and forth between server and players (when the driver gets out, another player comes close, and so on). Each handoff causes stutter and snapping. While the server owns the cart, the driver's inputs travel to the server and back, which feels laggy. Fix: when Seat.Occupant changes, the server calls cartRoot:SetNetworkOwner(player) for the driver (any part of the assembly; check CanSetNetworkOwnership first). When the seat is empty, call SetNetworkOwner(nil) or SetNetworkOwnershipAuto(). Anchored parts cannot be owned. Kill brick: when a client owns the cart, the server only sees positions the client reports, delayed. Touched events on the server fire for those replicated, interpolated positions, so they can fire late or oddly, and an exploiter can fake them. Make the kill logic check what touched it (a character Humanoid, not cart parts) and validate it, or use server-side spatial queries.

I am not fully sure of the exact names. As I understand it, Roblox added separate include and exclude instance lists so that one query can carry both (for example lists like IncludeInstances / ExcludeInstances), instead of a single FilterDescendantsInstances list whose meaning depends on FilterType (Include or Exclude, never both). Exclusion takes priority over inclusion, and the old pair still works for compatibility. With the new lists:
```lua
local p = RaycastParams.new()
-- new-style: include Map, exclude Map.Glass (exclude wins)
-- p.<IncludeList> = {workspace.Map}; p.<ExcludeList> = {workspace.Map.Glass}
```
Portable fallback with the classic API: FilterType = Include, FilterDescendantsInstances = {workspace.Map}, then if the result's Instance is a descendant of Map.Glass (or is Glass), cast again from just past the hit point, adding a small offset. Alternatively, put the glass in a collision group and set p.CollisionGroup so the glass is skipped.

E23:
From what I understand (check the API reference for exact details): MarketplaceService:BindReceiptHandler(productId, handler) registers a handler for one developer product ID. The handler is called with the receiptInfo table (PlayerId, ProductId, PurchaseId, CurrencySpent, PlaceIdWherePurchased...) and must return Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.PurchaseGranted once it has granted the item and saved it, or NotProcessedYet to have the purchase retried later. Errors or yields that fail count as not processed. Each script binds only its own products, so separate systems (gems, revives, boosts) no longer fight over the single ProcessReceipt callback, which can only be assigned once. The method probably returns a connection or unbinder for cleanup. Do not mix the two models for the same product; a bound handler takes priority, and ProcessReceipt can serve as a fallback for products nobody bound, depending on the documented rules.
```lua
local MPS = game:GetService("MarketplaceService")
MPS:BindReceiptHandler(1234567, function(receipt)
  local player = game.Players:GetPlayerByUserId(receipt.PlayerId)
  if not player then return Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.NotProcessedYet end
  local ok = grantGems(player, 100, receipt.PurchaseId) -- idempotent, saved
  return ok and Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.PurchaseGranted or Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.NotProcessedYet
end)
```
Granting must be idempotent: record each PurchaseId so a retried receipt is not granted twice.
E24: Luau's math library gained math.lerp(a: number, b: number, t: number): number, which returns a + (b - a) * t and gives exactly b at t = 1. It also gained math.isnan(x), math.isinf(x) and math.isfinite(x). math.map(x: number, inMin: number, inMax: number, outMin: number, outMax: number): number, which remaps x from [inMin, inMax] to [outMin, outMax] without clamping, was added slightly earlier and sits alongside these. Older helpers still useful: math.clamp, math.sign, math.round, math.noise. The vector library also gained vector.lerp and related functions. Use these built-ins (they are fast-pathed) instead of hand-written local lerp or map functions.
